summary:
FirePulse Decision Lab turns NASA MODIS and VIIRS observations into a harmonized fire-activity calendar for environmental analysts and land managers. Its Kazakhstan benchmark covers 2003–2025 and helps users compare seasons, investigate unusual months, review recurring locations and measure mapped burned hectares.

Observations are compared on a shared equal-area grid, with sensor calibration evaluated on held-out years. In a separate monthly FRP comparison, calibration reduced mean absolute error by 43.3% for Kazakhstan in 2023–2025. Interactive cases distinguish known persistent thermal sources from unverified candidates, reveal seasonal shifts and place historical anomalies alongside ERA5 weather context. NASA MCD64A1 supplies burned-area measurements independently of hotspot counts.

A separate global explorer supports a dated NOAA-21 snapshot, FIRMS CSV import and user-initiated API requests. Four guided cases, downloadable CSV/GeoJSON, source code and documented methods make the evidence inspectable and reproducible. FirePulse supports decisions about where and when to investigate; it does not claim operational fire forecasting or worldwide validation of its regional calibration.
details:
Live application: https://steppe-fire-calendar-super161.meremonad5.chatgpt.site/?lang=en

Source code, benchmark data and methods: https://steppe-fire-calendar-super161.meremonad5.chatgpt.site/download?bundle=source&lang=en

PURPOSE AND USERS

FirePulse Decision Lab helps environmental analysts and land managers decide which periods and locations deserve closer investigation. It addresses the challenge of combining MODIS and VIIRS records into a usable fire-activity calendar while preserving the differences between sensors. Kazakhstan is the benchmark case study, with Kostanay and Mangystau providing contrasting examples of seasonal burning and persistent thermal sources.

HOW IT WORKS

The historical benchmark uses MODIS Aqua observations from 2003–2025 and VIIRS S-NPP observations from 2013–2025. Its main calendar includes 1,809,628 selected presumed vegetation-fire observations. Records are mapped to an equal-area grid: for each sensor, a 1 km cell observed as active more than once in the same UTC day contributes one active cell-day. This reduces repeated-observation effects without presenting detections as individual fires or hectares.

A regional MODIS-to-VIIRS scaling factor is trained on 2013–2022. The complete years 2023–2025 are reserved for evaluation. Relative to the unscaled common-grid baseline, held-out monthly activity MAE decreases by 67.3% for Kazakhstan and 58.6% for Kostanay. These results measure improved agreement between sensors, not independent ground-truth wildfire accuracy.

FRP is evaluated separately as radiative power. In the monthly observation-sum experiment, calibration reduces Kazakhstan's held-out MAE by 43.3%. Monthly FRP observation sums depend on sampling and are not fire energy. A separate matched-time experiment, uncertainty and sensitivity checks are available in the methodology.

DECISIONS SUPPORTED BY THE DEMO

Four guided cases lead from a question to inspectable evidence. Users can compare sensors, screen persistent-source observations, examine changes in seasonal timing and investigate an unusual historical month alongside weather context.

In Mangystau, the 2025 screening case starts with 846 observations. Removing NASA type 2 records leaves 170; additionally hiding unverified temporal candidates leaves 110. The two filters remain separate so candidates are not presented as confirmed industrial sources.

Equal-year MODIS Aqua profiles for 2003–2012 and 2016–2025 show that Kazakhstan's first 10% of observed annual activity accumulates 13 days earlier, with a 95% year-bootstrap range from 22 to 1 days earlier. This supports seasonal monitoring questions without attributing the change to climate.

A fixed 10 km recurrence grid identifies 98 cells with selected observations in every one of the 23 years. It describes repeated observations, not the number of fires or proof of illegal burning. Historical anomalies can be compared with ERA5 weather sampled at five Kostanay reference points; the interface does not turn weather coincidence into a causal diagnosis.

BURNED AREA AND GLOBAL PORTABILITY

NASA MCD64A1.061 BurnDate and QA rasters provide separate mapped burned-area measurements for all twelve months of 2022 in Kostanay. September contains approximately 95,117 hectares of regional mapped burning. QA-valid spatial support covers 99.35% of the study area; this percentage is not a classification-accuracy score. Areas use native sinusoidal pixel areas and fractional intersections with the regional boundary.

A separate worldwide explorer contains a real NOAA-21 snapshot retrieved on 14 November 2026 with 77,261 observations. The snapshot is dated and does not automatically refresh. Users can import FIRMS CSV files, choose a region and export CSV, GeoJSON and provenance. An optional FIRMS Area API connector accepts the visitor's key; a successful request with a real user MAP_KEY has not yet been verified. These recent observations do not extend the historical regional calibration or establish operational early-warning readiness.

CREATIVITY, TOOLS AND REPRODUCIBILITY

The contribution is a connected decision workflow: calendar, sensor comparison, seasonal profile, recurrence, source screening, weather context and burned hectares. Each result retains its unit, source, period and scope. Guided cases make the first interaction useful, while expandable methods preserve the scientific detail.

The application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet. Python processing uses NumPy, pandas, Rasterio, Shapely and pyproj. NASA FIRMS and MCD64A1 are combined with ERA5 via Open-Meteo, geoBoundaries administrative geometry and OpenStreetMap basemaps; MCD64A1 rasters were accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer.

The public package includes code, tests, derived datasets, all 276 monthly map layers, provenance, checksums, methodological notes and the seven-slide presentation. Original FirePulse code is Apache-2.0; third-party data and software retain their own licenses. Validation and limitations are documented so others can reproduce and challenge the results.

AI ASSISTANCE

OpenAI assistants substantially authored code, tests, research notes and draft text under Alua Akhmetkali's direction. Satellite and weather inputs are real source data; numerical results are calculated by reproducible code. AI assistance is disclosed in the public source package and metadata. Automated tests and scientific validation are documented; complete independent human review remains pending.
